## Two kinds of aim {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**What I want you to understand**

- What reproducibility, robustness and replicability each mean, and why they come apart
- Why analysts disagree – and how much of that is disagreement about the *question*
- What a causal graph is good for when you cannot make a causal claim
- What a multiverse shows, and what it cannot show
- What preregistration settles, and what it leaves open
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**What I want you to be able to do**

- Get an analysis running from someone else's materials
- Write an estimand in one sentence, and a DAG that matches it
- Reproduce a published result to the third decimal
- Vary a specification one choice at a time and read what changed
- Preregister an analysis before you run it, and report where it ranks among the alternatives
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
Two columns, because the course has two kinds of aim. On the left is what I want you to understand – conceptual work, and most of it is not about code at all. On the right is what I want you to be able to do, and every one of those is something you will have done at least once with your own hands before we finish. If you only take the left-hand column home you will have heard some interesting arguments and changed nothing about your practice. If you only take the right-hand column you will have learned some R. What I want is the two together, because the concepts tell you which of the things you can now do is worth doing.
:::

## What you do not need {#what-you-do-not-need-today}

::: {.none}
- No git, and no GitHub account
- No OSF account – we will read OSF, not log into it
- No working installation yet: the browser lab runs R inside the web page, and Task 1 sets yours up
- Nothing to sign up for; nothing leaves your machine except the results you choose to submit
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Do this now:** open your workspace folder in your IDE, and open the browser lab in a tab beside it; R loads in the page while we talk.
:::

::: notes
Before anything else, a word on what you do not need. You do not need git, or a GitHub account, or an OSF account – we will look at OSF from the outside, like readers. If your installation is not working yet, that is fine: the browser lab runs R inside the page itself, and the first hands-on task gets everybody set up properly. One thing to do right now, while I talk. Open the workspace folder in your IDE, then open the browser lab in a tab beside it and just leave it. R loads in the background there, so it will be ready long before you need it. If you are on the call with one screen, the setup page has a tip: put the meeting on your phone or a second window and keep your IDE full-screen.
:::
